1_58.probe: In the paper 'The Era of 1-bit LLMs: All Large Language Models are in 1.58 Bits', the logarithmic expression (in base 2) that corresponds to the 1.58 bits claimed for a ternary weight is $\log_2(3)$
1_58.excerpt: A weight that can take three distinct values (for example \{-1,0,+1\}) carries \log_2(3) bits of information.

1_58.probe: In the paper 'The Era of 1-bit LLMs: All Large Language Models are in 1.58 Bits', the logarithmic expression (in base 2) that corresponds to the 1.58 bits claimed for a ternary weight is $\log_2(3)$
1_58.excerpt:
Bits measure information. If a variable can take N equally likely states, its information content is log2(N) bits. Ternary weights have three possible values, so the per-weight information is

$ \log_2(3) \approx 1.585\ \text{bits}. $

1_58.probe: In the paper 'The Era of 1-bit LLMs: All Large Language Models are in 1.58 Bits', the RoundClip operation is defined to bound quantized values to a fixed interval and thus enforces that quantized values are clamped to $[-1, 1]$

According to the paper 'The Era of 1-bit LLMs: All Large Language Models are in 1.58 Bits', conceptually the quantity $\gamma$, defined as $\gamma = \frac{1}{nm}\sum_{ij} |W_{ij}|$, in the absmean quantization function  which divides $W$ by $\gamma + \epsilon$ before applying $\mathrm{RoundClip}(\cdot, -1, 1)$ to produce values in $\{-1, 0, +1\}$  acts as a scaling factor
1_58.excerpt: Intuitively, \gamma captures a typical magnitude in the matrix; dividing by it normalizes the distribution so that large coefficients map to \(\pm 1\), small ones map to 0, and intermediate ones are rounded to the nearest ternary symbol.

1_58.probe: In the paper 'The Era of 1-bit LLMs: All Large Language Models are in 1.58 Bits', the logarithmic expression (in base 2) that corresponds to the 1.58 bits claimed for a ternary weight is $\log_2(3)$
1_58.excerpt: Short answer: "$1.58$ bits" is the information-theoretic cost per weight ($\log_2(3) \approx 1.585$) because each weight takes one of three values $\{-1,0,+1\}$.

BOFT.probe: In the paper 'Parameter-Efficient Orthogonal Finetuning via Factorization', the Cayley parameterization is written as $\bm{R}=(\bm{I}+\bm{Q})(\bm{I}-\bm{Q})^{-1}$. The constraint required on $\bm{Q}$ so that $\bm{R}$ remains orthogonal is that $\bm{Q}$ be skew-symmetric
BOFT.excerpt: To ensure \bm{R} remains orthogonal during optimization, OFT uses a parameterization such as the Cayley transform: express \bm{R} = (\bm{I} + \bm{Q})(\bm{I} - \bm{Q})^{-1}, where \bm{Q} is skew-symmetric (\bm{Q}^\top = -\bm{Q}).

BOFT.probe: In the paper 'Parameter-Efficient Orthogonal Finetuning via Factorization', the Cayley parameterization is written as $\bm{R}=(\bm{I}+\bm{Q})(\bm{I}-\bm{Q})^{-1}$. The constraint required on $\bm{Q}$ so that $\bm{R}$ remains orthogonal is that $\bm{Q}$ be skew-symmetric
BOFT.excerpt: The paper uses the Cayley transform $\mathbf{R}=(\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{Q})(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{Q})^{-1}$ with $\mathbf{Q}^\top=-\mathbf{Q}$ to parameterize each orthogonal block.

BOFT.probe: In the paper 'Parameter-Efficient Orthogonal Finetuning via Factorization', the Cayley parameterization is written as $\bm{R}=(\bm{I}+\bm{Q})(\bm{I}-\bm{Q})^{-1}$. The constraint required on $\bm{Q}$ so that $\bm{R}$ remains orthogonal is that $\bm{Q}$ be skew-symmetric
BOFT.excerpt:
The Cayley parameterization represents an orthogonal matrix R in terms of a skew-symmetric matrix Q (i.e., Q^T = −Q) as follows:

R = (I + Q)(I − Q)^{-1},

assuming (I − Q) is invertible. When Q is skew-symmetric, this formula maps Q to an orthogonal matrix R (except when −1 is an eigenvalue that makes (I − Q) singular).

BOFT.probe: According to the paper 'Parameter-Efficient Orthogonal Finetuning via Factorization', for fixed $d$ and $m$, the effective number of trainable parameters is given by $\frac{1}{2}(b-1)dm$, so to minimize this quantity one should decrease $b
BOFT.excerpt: Parameter cost estimate: a BOFT(m,b) layer costs about \tfrac{1}{2}(b-1) d m effective parameters for a linear layer of size d×n. With b=2 and m=log d, that becomes O(d log d), much smaller than O(d^2).

BOFT.probe: According to the paper 'Parameter-Efficient Orthogonal Finetuning via Factorization', the asymptotic number of trainable parameters per layer for BOFT, expressed in terms of $d$, is $\mathcal{O}(d\log d)$
BOFT.excerpt: By constraining each sparse factor to be orthogonal (which can be enforced via small block orthogonal parameterizations such as 2\times2 rotations with Cayley transform), BOFT attains an orthogonal parameterization with only \mathcal{O}(d\log d) trainable parameters for the butterfly case (m=\log d, block size b=2).

QLoRA.probe: In the paper 'QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs', the authors halved the learning rate and doubled the batch size for larger models to stabilize training
QLoRA.excerpt: The QLoRA experiments used a consistent finetuning procedure (NF4 QLoRA, cross-entropy supervised objective, same general LoRA configuration) across datasets and model sizes. The authors note that most hyperparameters found at the 7B scale generalize (including number of epochs), except learning rate and batch size, for which they make modest scale-dependent adjustments (they halve the LR and double batch size for 33B/65B).

QLoRA.probe: In the paper 'QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs', the authors halved the learning rate and doubled the batch size for larger models to stabilize training
QLoRA.excerpt: When moving to 33B and 65B, the authors halved the learning rate and doubled the batch size relative to the 7B settings that worked.

QLoRA.probe: In the paper 'QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs', the authors attribute the recovery of performance after quantization primarily to the LoRA adapters
QLoRA.excerpt: Store the pretrained model in very low precision (4-bit), keep those weights frozen, and backpropagate gradients through them into small, trainable LoRA adapters. The frozen, quantized base plus tiny adapters give you full 16-bit quality at a tiny fraction of the memory cost.

QLoRA.probe: In the paper 'QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs', the distributional property of pretrained weights that underlies NF4's information-theoretic optimality is that they are zero-mean normal
QLoRA.excerpt: NF4 is a 4-bit data type designed to be information-theoretically optimal for zero-mean normally distributed weights.

QLoRA.probe: According to the paper 'QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs', when scoring paired responses, GPT-4 exhibited a systematic bias, specifically favoring the earlier response
QLoRA.excerpt: Evaluation nuances: GPT-4 and human evaluation mostly agree on rankings but have systematic differences and biases (e.g., order effects when prompting GPT-4).

DPO.probe: According to the paper 'Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model', conceptually the term $\beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}$ in DPO's formulation plays the role of an implicit reward
DPO.excerpt:
A central conceptual move in Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is to treat the policy itself as defining an implicit reward. Concretely, for a parametrized policy \(\pi_\theta(y\mid x)\) and a fixed reference policy \(\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)\), DPO defines an implicit reward function
\[\hat r_\theta(x,y) \;=\; \beta \log\frac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}.\]

DPO.probe: In the paper 'Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model', to optimize a policy directly from preference data instead of doing reward estimation followed by RL, DPO trains the policy using a simple supervised loss, namely binary cross-entropy
DPO.excerpt:
Having expressed the BT preference probability in terms of a policy, we can write a maximum likelihood objective for a parametric policy \(\pi_\theta\). Given a dataset of human comparisons ... the log-likelihood under the BT model (with the reparameterized reward) becomes a binary cross-entropy loss over the policy log‑ratio differences:
\[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DPO}}(\pi_\theta;\pi_{\text{ref}}) = -\mathbb{E}_{(x,y_w,y_l)\sim\mathcal{D}}\bigl[\log\sigma\bigl(\beta\log\tfrac{\pi_\theta(y_w\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w\mid x)} - \beta\log\tfrac{\pi_\theta(y_l\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l\mid x)}\bigr)\bigr].\]

DPO.probe: In the paper 'Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model', the Bradley-Terry two-item comparison model, which can be written as $p^*(y_1\triangleright y_2\\mid x)=\frac{\exp\bigl(r(x,y_1)\bigr)}{\exp\bigl(r(x,y_1)\bigr)+\exp\bigl(r(x,y_2)\bigr)}$ and equivalently as $p^*(y_1\succ y_2\mid x)=\sigma\left(r(x,y_1)-r(x,y_2)\right)$, is mathematically analogous to the common binary statistical model known as logistic regression
DPO.excerpt:
The Bradley–Terry (BT) model is the simplest useful special case for pairwise comparisons. If two completions \(y_1\) and \(y_2\) are presented for the same prompt \(x\), the BT model writes the probability that \(y_1\) is preferred to \(y_2\) as
\[p^*(y_1 \succ y_2 \mid x) = \frac{\exp\bigl(r^*(x,y_1)\bigr)}{\exp\bigl(r^*(x,y_1)\bigr) + \exp\bigl(r^*(x,y_2)\bigr)}.\]
This has the convenient form of a logistic function of the score difference:
\[p^*(y_1 \succ y_2 \mid x) = \sigma\bigl(r^*(x,y_1) - r^*(x,y_2)\bigr),\]
where \(\sigma(z)=1/(1+e^{-z})\).

DPO.probe: According to the paper 'Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model', conceptually the term $\beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}$ in DPO's formulation plays the role of an implicit reward
DPO.excerpt: The implicit reward is defined by $\hat r_\theta(x,y)=\beta \log\frac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_\text{ref}(y\mid x)}$.

DPO.probe: According to the paper 'Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model', conceptually the term $\beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}$ in DPO's formulation plays the role of an implicit reward
DPO.excerpt: DPO implicitly defines a reward \hat r_\theta via the policy — so if you later want a standalone reward model, you could extract it, but the main point is you do not need to train one explicitly to get a good policy.

GRPO.probe: In the paper 'DeepSeekMath: Pushing the Limits of Mathematical Reasoning in Open Language Models', the authors attribute DeepSeekMath's improved mathematical reasoning to two key factors: data selection and GRPO
GRPO.excerpt:
The two technical levers that mattered

1) Large, carefully filtered math pre-training data (DeepSeekMath Corpus) ...

2) An efficient RL algorithm tailored for comparison-style rewards: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO).

GRPO.probe: In the paper 'DeepSeekMath: Pushing the Limits of Mathematical Reasoning in Open Language Models', when the authors report 'Self-consistency over $64$ samples from DeepSeekMath~7B achieves $60.9\%$ on MATH', the self-consistency mechanism is most likely implementing a majority vote
GRPO.excerpt: Self-consistency: sample many independent chain-of-thought outputs (here 64), compute the answer for each, and pick the majority answer (a simple ensemble over decoded traces). Self-consistency often increases accuracy for reasoning tasks by aggregating multiple probable solution paths.

GRPO.probe: According to the paper 'DeepSeekMath: Pushing the Limits of Mathematical Reasoning in Open Language Models', GRPO removes the expensive component used by PPO that causes substantial memory and computation burden, the value function
GRPO.excerpt: the authors state that Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) forgoes the critic/value function and estimates baselines from group scores, reducing training resource demands; the paper explicitly claims this reduces which resource compared to PPO? memory usage

GRPO.probe: In the paper 'DeepSeekMath: Pushing the Limits of Mathematical Reasoning in Open Language Models', GRPO was applied using only a subset of English instruction tuning data yet improved a Chinese benchmark ($\text{CMATH}$), demonstrating cross-lingual transfer
GRPO.excerpt: GRPO was applied to DeepSeekMath-Instruct 7B using only a subset of English instruction-tuning data (chain-of-thought-format GSM8K and MATH questions, about 144K examples). Additional empirical notes from the paper: - GRPO also improved out-of-domain math benchmarks (e.g., CMATH improved from 84.6% → 88.8%).

GRPO.probe: In the paper 'DeepSeekMath: Pushing the Limits of Mathematical Reasoning in Open Language Models', the authors attribute DeepSeekMath's improved mathematical reasoning to two key factors: data selection and GRPO
GRPO.excerpt:
Two technical pillars drive the DeepSeekMath approach.

The first is large-scale, targeted pre-training on math-rich web data. ... The second pillar is Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), an algorithmic variant of PPO tailored for LLM fine-tuning with reward models.

OFT.probe: According to the paper 'Controlling Text-to-Image Diffusion by Orthogonal Finetuning', compared to additive low-rank updates like LoRA, OFT modifies weights multiplicatively
OFT.excerpt: OFT is multiplicative rather than additive. It learns a layer-shared orthogonal matrix \;R\; that left-multiplies a pretrained weight matrix \;W^0\; so that the finetuned weight is \;W = R W^0\;.

OFT.probe: In the paper 'Controlling Text-to-Image Diffusion by Orthogonal Finetuning', the authors explain that OFT achieves parameter efficiency by exploiting a sparsity-inducing structure in its orthogonal parameterization, namely block-diagonal orthogonality
OFT.excerpt: - Block-diagonal $\mathbf{R}$. Instead of a full $d\times d$ orthogonal matrix, use $\mathbf{R} = \text{diag}(R_1, ..., R_r)$ with smaller blocks. This cuts parameter and compute cost while maintaining orthogonality in each block.

OFT.probe: According to the paper 'Controlling Text-to-Image Diffusion by Orthogonal Finetuning', the ablation shows that the specific constraint that primarily prevents model collapse in OFT is the orthogonality constraint
OFT.excerpt: Empirically (Figure referenced in the paper), removing the orthogonality constraint led to failed finetuning: the model produced unrealistic images and did not achieve the intended control effect.

OFT.probe: According to the paper 'Controlling Text-to-Image Diffusion by Orthogonal Finetuning', the ablation shows that the specific constraint that primarily prevents model collapse in OFT is the orthogonality constraint
OFT.excerpt: Short answer: it fails because removing orthogonality removes the single thing that (1) exactly preserves the pairwise neuron angles/hyperspherical energy and (2) strongly regularizes the transform so finetuning stays on a benign manifold.

OFT.probe: According to the paper 'Controlling Text-to-Image Diffusion by Orthogonal Finetuning', viewed geometrically, learning a layer-shared orthogonal matrix $\mathbf{R}$ amounts to changing the coordinate system
OFT.excerpt: Short answer: No — algebraically a single OFT layer is equivalent to a learned orthogonal change of basis on that layer’s input, but taken across a real network (nonlinearities, residuals, attention) learning one orthogonal matrix per layer is not reducible to a single global basis change and therefore is expressive enough to adapt the model.
